At C, D and E. All three lie on flat land on the valley floor, close to the river or the lake.

The chapter gives the reason: physical factors like relief, altitude, soils, climate, drainage and groundwater level influence the type and spacing of settlements, and where water is a crucial factor houses are situated along the water source. Flat ground can be built on and cultivated, and the river and lake supply water.

Of the three, E and C sit on green land a little back from the water, which is safer than D, which is on the sandy ground at the very edge of the water and would be the first to flood.

At A. It lies high on a bare, steep mountain slope that is still under snow.

Nothing there favours settlement. The slope is too steep to build on or cultivate, the altitude and the cold make habitation difficult, there is no soil cover, and the water is locked up as snow rather than available as a stream. The chapter lists relief, altitude, soils, climate, drainage and groundwater level among the physical factors that decide where settlements form, and this site is unfavourable on every one of them.

B is the next least likely, because although it is vegetated it is still a hill slope rather than level ground.

The photograph shows four of them at work.

Relief: the level valley floor can be built on and cultivated, while the steep slopes above cannot.

Availability of water: the river running down the valley and the lake at its foot supply the settlements near them. The chapter notes that in dry regions water is a crucial factor and houses are situated along the water source.

Soils and vegetation: the green valley floor indicates soil cover that will support cultivation, whereas the bare rock higher up will not.

Altitude and climate: the lower ground is warmer and free of snow, so it is habitable through the year.

The chapter groups these as the physical factors, and adds that cultural and economic factors also affect human settlements.

Yes. The chapter states that physical, cultural and economic factors affect human settlements, so the economic ones stand alongside the physical ones rather than behind them.

Its reasoning is that a settlement is not only a place to build houses. The chapter says a settlement shows that a group of people are using some territory to build houses as well as for their economic support, and that man stays there, lives and carries out economic activities. A site with good physical conditions but no means of livelihood will not hold people.

In the photograph, the flat valley floor offers cultivable land and the river offers water and a route, both of which are economic as much as physical advantages.

Yes. The chapter says settlements are developed due to the co-relation between man and environment, so the physical setting shapes what people can do there as well as where they can live.

In the photograph the level, well-watered valley floor allows cultivation and grazing, while the bare snow-covered slopes above allow neither. The river permits fishing and movement along the valley. Had the same people settled at A, none of those activities would be open to them.

The same relationship runs through the chapter's treatment of land use: in rural areas land use revolves around agriculture, and which land can be cultivated at all is decided by relief, soil and water.

The chapter groups the factors that affect the development of settlements into three kinds.

Physical factors: relief, altitude, soils, climate, drainage and groundwater level. These influence both the type and the spacing of settlements, and where water is scarce they decide the position of the houses themselves.

Social and cultural factors: the chapter notes that social bonding and social needs bring people together in one place, and that social factors can also lead to the fragmentation of settlements. It gives security as an example, since areas that were frequently conquered or attacked by outsiders favoured the evolution of nucleated settlements.

Economic factors: a settlement exists for economic support as well as for shelter, so the means of livelihood available at a site help decide whether people stay.

Yes. The chapter divides settlements on the basis of their functions into two types, rural and urban.

Urban settlements are generally compact and larger in size than rural ones. In rural areas land use revolves around agriculture, whereas in urban areas it revolves around residential and other economic activities. The chapter's later account adds that rural areas are those where people are mainly engaged in primary activities and urban areas those where the majority of the working population is engaged in non-primary activities.

Urban settlements can be classified further, into towns, cities, metropolitan cities, mega cities, urban agglomerations and outgrowths, and by their dominant function.

A town can be known for one function, but it does not carry out only one.

The chapter puts it directly: some towns and cities specialise in certain functions and are known for some specific activities, products or services, however each town performs a number of functions. Cities are classified by their dominant or specialised function, not by their only one.

Cities become multi-functional as they grow. The chapter says cities generally carry out more than one function as they grow, that one of these may be a major one, and that as towns become cities and cities become metro cities the complexity of a city increases with time. A growing population needs housing, transport, education, health care, administration and trade, so new functions are added to whatever the settlement began as.

The chapter adds that these changes show themselves in the land use and structure of the city, and even in its skyline.

It is called the rural-urban fringe.

The chapter defines it as the area between urban and rural area, which has characteristics of both. It is not a separate zone as such, but a transition between the two that merges into both of them. The term has been used to designate areas where there is a mixture of rural and urban land use.

The chapter adds that when large urban areas develop and the span of the urban area increases, the process is called urban sprawl, and that beyond the urban fringe lies the rural fringe, consisting of villages only and partly affected by urbanisation.

The index shows twelve classes, each with its own colour.

| Colour | Land use / land cover class |
|---|---|
| Pale yellow | Agriculture |
| Olive green | Forest |
| Light pink (mauve) | Wasteland-Scrub |
| Blue | Waterbodies |
| Dark red | Built Up - Rural |
| Bright pink (magenta) | Built Up - Residential |
| Salmon | Built Up - Residential-Sparse |
| Navy blue | Built Up - Industrial |
| Purple | Built Up - Public/Semipublic |
| Dark green | Built Up - Recreation |
| Brown | Built Up - Mining/Quarry |
| Pale teal | Built Up - Open Space |

Eight of the twelve are built-up classes, which is what makes the map useful for watching a city grow.

The blue line is the Panchaganaga River, which runs across the south-east corner of both maps. Blue is the colour given to waterbodies in the index.

The black lines are the roads, which form a network across the map and meet at Ichalkaranji and at the villages around it. They are drawn as plain lines rather than in a legend colour, because a road is shown as a line feature and not as an area of land cover.
The Panchaganaga River.

Any two of the settlements named around the city, for example Rui and Chandur.

The others shown are Sajani, Korochi, Takawade, Ingali, Haroli, Jambhali, Nandani, Kondigre, Yadrav, Mangaonwadi, Gaon Bhag and Shahu Nagar.
Ichalkaranji, in Kolhapur district. The title printed on the maps is LAND USE LAND COVER MAP - ICHALKARANJI CITY, KOLHAPUR DISTRICT.
Map A) belongs to 2007 and map B) to 2017, so the pair covers a span of ten years.

Agriculture, shown in pale yellow, and Wasteland-Scrub, shown in light pink, have both reduced.

They have reduced in the same places, around the edges of Ichalkaranji, because that is where the bright pink residential area has spread over them between 2007 and 2017.

This is the process the chapter describes when it says that plot layouts are usually located on the periphery of urban areas and that these lands encroach the agricultural land due to the pressure of the increasing population.

Built Up - Residential, shown in bright pink, has increased most, spreading outward from Ichalkaranji in every direction.

Built Up - Industrial, shown in navy blue, has also grown, at both of the areas marked INDUSTRIAL ESTATE, and a brown Built Up - Mining/Quarry patch appears in the north-west that was not there in 2007.

Taken together the map shows the transition the chapter describes, in which land passes from agriculture and wasteland into residential and industrial use as an urban area expands.

Because becoming urban depends on what a settlement does, not merely on how long it exists.

The chapter divides settlements by function into rural and urban, and notes that rural areas are those where people are mainly engaged in primary activities while urban areas are those where the majority of the working population is engaged in non-primary activities. A village whose people remain in agriculture stays rural however long it grows.

Size and compactness follow from that. Urban settlements are generally compact and larger in size, and the chapter's classification runs from town through city, metropolitan city and mega city, each step needing more population and more non-primary work than the last.

The physical setting limits which villages can make the change at all. Relief, altitude, soils, climate, drainage and groundwater level influence the type and spacing of settlements, so a village hemmed in by hills or short of water cannot grow into a city even if its people wished it.

The chapter's own examples show which ones do change. Bhandup, Kalyan and Virar became suburbs because Mumbai grew towards them, and Wakad and Hinjawadi because Pune did. A village far from any such growth has no comparable pull.

Because agriculture is what rural people do, and land use follows the economic activity of the people using the land.

The chapter states that generally in rural areas land use revolves around agriculture, while in urban areas it revolves around residential and other economic activities. It also defines rural areas as those where people are mainly engaged in primary activities.

The classification of rural land use makes the same point by its shape. Of the nine categories used by the Land Record Department, most are agricultural or defined by their relation to cultivation: area under permanent pastures and grazing lands, area under miscellaneous tree crops and groves, culturable waste-land, current fallow, fallow other than current fallow, and net area sown. Only forests, non-agricultural uses, and barren and wastelands fall outside that.

Even the categories that are not cultivated are defined by whether they could be. Culturable waste-land is land left fallow for more than five years that can be brought under cultivation after reclamation, while barren and wasteland normally cannot be brought under cultivation with the available technology.

Because the fringe is a transition rather than a boundary.

The chapter defines the rural-urban fringe as the area between urban and rural area, and says it is not a separate zone as such but a transition between the two that merges into both of them. The term designates areas where there is a mixture of rural and urban land use.

Its administration is mixed. The city and surrounding areas consist essentially of two types of administrative area, the Municipal Councils and the Gram Panchayats, so both kinds of local government operate within the fringe.

Its land use is mixed. Agricultural land may have been converted to residential or industrial areas, or a part of the area may be entirely rural, with the only link to the city being the daily commuters.

Even its towns are mixed. The smaller municipal towns close to the main city tend to lose their identity and are in reality part of the geographical city, with services comparable to the main city, while towns further away keep a distinct identity and have inferior services and their own problems of urban amenities and transportation.

The people living there behave in both ways too: they use automobiles to make daily trips into the central area where their offices and economic institutions are located, while living outside the city proper.

Because a city can only grow by taking land into new uses, so growth and land use change together.

The chapter states that as towns become cities and cities become metro cities, complexity increases and lots of changes can be seen in them, and that these changes are in the form of change in land use and structure of a city, even changing the skyline.

The direction of the change is outward. Plot layouts are vacant lands mostly developed for construction of buildings, usually located on the periphery of the urban areas, and these lands encroach the agricultural land due to the pressure of the increasing population. The Ichalkaranji maps show exactly this between 2007 and 2017, with residential land spreading over what had been agriculture and wasteland-scrub.

Growth also multiplies the kinds of land use. An expanding city needs residential, industrial, institutional, recreational, transportation and commercial areas, and where they occur together the chapter calls the result mixed land use.

Beyond the built-up edge, growth produces the rural-urban fringe, and when large urban areas develop and the span of the urban area increases, the chapter calls that urban sprawl.

Rural and urban settlements are two types of one thing, divided by function, and they depend on each other.

The chapter divides settlements on the basis of their functions into rural and urban, with rural areas those where people are mainly engaged in primary activities and urban areas those where the majority of the working population is engaged in non-primary activities. Land use follows: around agriculture in the one, around residential and other economic activities in the other.

They are joined physically by the rural-urban fringe, which has characteristics of both and merges into each. Within it the smaller municipal towns close to the main city lose their identity and become part of the geographical city, while the areas further out stay rural, their only link with the city being the daily commuters who travel in to the offices and economic institutions at the centre.

They are joined by growth. When a city expands, nearby settlements become its suburbs: the chapter gives Bhandup, Kalyan and Virar for Mumbai, and Wakad and Hinjawadi for Pune. These are cities in themselves but developed as a result of growth in the main city.

They are joined by land. Urban expansion takes agricultural land on the periphery for plot layouts, so the growth of the one is at the cost of the other.

And they are joined by scale of service. Larger settlements have a sphere of influence affecting the surrounding settlements, so a village with one or two general stores depends on a larger town for what it does not have.

The chapter groups the problems of urban settlements under several heads: economic, social, cultural, environmental, infrastructural, and governance and administrative.

The problems it describes in its own account are mostly those of growth outrunning provision. Housing, water supply and transportation may prove insufficient as compared to the population. Lack of housing leads to an increase in slums. Public facilities get affected very badly. Economic inequality rises in such cities, and crime rates may also increase.

There are problems of land as well. A large chunk of agricultural land in the peripheral regions is used for non-agricultural purposes like housing, and prices of land increase tremendously.

The fringe brings problems of its own. Towns away from the main city maintain a distinct identity but have a distinct set of problems relating to urban amenities and transportation, and the quality of these services is generally inferior to that of the main city.

[Note: the chapter lists the six categories of urban problems as headings in an activity for the student to fill in from their own city, and does not itself give an example under each, so the problems above are drawn from its running account rather than from that table.]

Outside a metro city there may be a small town, or a number of well-established towns or small cities. These are called suburbs.

The chapter's examples are Bhandup, Kalyan and Virar, which are considered suburbs of the main city of Mumbai, and Wakad and Hinjawadi, which are suburbs of Pune.

The point the chapter makes about them is that they are all cities in themselves, but developed as a result of growth in the main city. They are therefore called its suburbs, not because they are small, but because their growth came from the city beside them.

Suburbs belong to the wider process of urban sprawl, which the chapter describes as what happens when large urban areas develop and the span of urban areas increases.

Mixed land use is an area where various types of land uses exist together.

The chapter explains that these may include residential, commercial and industrial land use in an integrated manner, and that in such areas one can find houses, businesses, shops, schools, clinics and open spaces at one place itself.

It is one of the eight categories of urban land use the chapter lists, alongside residential, industrial, institutional, recreational, transportation, commercial and plot layouts.

It arises naturally as a city grows, because commercial areas are intermixed with residential areas, and only at a few places do commercial areas aggregate into definite clusters, especially at the core, that is the Central Business District.

The chapter describes rural settlements by their function, their land use, their size and their form.

Function. Rural settlements are those where people are mainly engaged in primary activities. The chapter notes that rural settlements can be classified further by function, such as proximity to farming, fishing and mining, and that a settlement focusing on one economic activity is called a single functional settlement.

Land use. In rural areas land use revolves around agriculture. The classification used by the Land Record Department is almost entirely agricultural: forests, non-agricultural uses, barren and wastelands, permanent pastures and grazing lands, miscellaneous tree crops and groves, culturable waste-land, current fallow, fallow other than current fallow, and net area sown.

Ownership. A distinctive feature is common land: most of the land under permanent pastures and grazing lands is owned by the village Panchayat or the Government, and what the Panchayat owns comes under Common Property Resources.

Size and spacing. Rural settlements are smaller and generally less compact than urban ones, which the chapter describes as generally compact and larger in size. They range from a hamlet upwards, and on the basis of spacing between the houses they may be compact or clustered or nucleated, semi-clustered or fragmented, dispersed, or isolated.

Services. Small settlements such as hamlets and villages have low populations and restricted access to services; a village may have only one or two general stores, which makes it a low-order service settlement dependent on a larger town nearby.

Setting. Physical factors such as relief, altitude, soils, climate, drainage and groundwater level influence their type and spacing, and where water is crucial the houses are situated along the water source.

A pattern is the spatial arrangement or distribution of settlements within a given area, and what produces one is usually some feature that the settlement has to arrange itself around.

A line in the landscape produces a linear pattern. The chapter says such settlements occur along a road, railway, canal or river, and lie in a straight line or take the shape of the road or the river.

Planning produces a rectangular pattern. Here settlements lie in straight lines that are parallel to each other, and the chapter notes that planned cities these days may take such a shape.

A central object produces a radial pattern. Settlements grow around a central object or centre, and that central point plays an important role in the development of the settlements around it.

A lake produces a circular pattern. Settlements take shape around the lake, and the houses are closely spaced because of the availability of water.

A meeting of lines or a coast produces a triangular pattern. The chapter places it at the confluence of two rivers or roads, or along a sea coast, where the settlement can grow on all three sides for physical or social reasons.

Unchecked growth produces no pattern at all. With the development of a settlement the population also increases, and increasing population leads to haphazard development, with houses built as per convenience and the space available.

One caution the chapter makes explicitly: a pattern is not a type. Compact settlement is a type of settlement, while linear settlement is a pattern, and a linear settlement can itself be compact or dispersed.

| Point of difference | Land use | Land cover |
|---|---|---|
| What it describes | The use that the land has been put to by people | The physical surface covering the land |
| Examples | Residential, industrial, institutional, recreational, transportation, commercial | Forest, water, ice, bare rock, sand |
| Whose act it records | Human activity on the land | The natural or built surface of the land |
| Can it be read from satellite imagery? | No, land use cannot be determined from satellite imagery alone | Yes, land cover can be determined by analysing satellite imagery |

The chapter warns that the two words are sometimes used synonymously but mean different things, and gives the case that separates them: the land use might be recreational while the land cover is vegetation or forest. It adds that understanding both together provides a comprehensive picture of a particular area.

| Point of difference | Barren and Wastelands | Non-agricultural Uses |
|---|---|---|
| What the land is | Land classified as wasteland, such as barren hilly terrains, desert lands and ravines | Land under settlements, both rural and urban, infrastructure such as roads and canals, industries and shops |
| Why it is not cultivated | It normally cannot be brought under cultivation with the available technology | It is not available for cultivation because it is already in use for something else |
| Is it in use? | No, it lies unused | Yes, it is in active use |
| What makes the category grow | It does not grow through human activity | An expansion in the secondary and tertiary activities would lead to an increase in this category |

Both are categories of the rural land-use classification used by the Land Record Department, and both fall outside the cultivated area, but for opposite reasons: one cannot be cultivated, the other is put to a different purpose.

| Point of difference | Radial pattern | Circular pattern |
|---|---|---|
| What the settlements grow around | A central object or centre | A lake |
| Role of the central feature | The central point plays an important role in the development of the settlements around it | The lake supplies water, which draws the houses to its edge |
| Shape produced | Settlements spread outward from the centre along the routes leading away from it | Settlements form a ring following the shore |
| Spacing of houses | Not stated by the chapter | Houses are closely spaced because of the availability of water |

Both patterns are organised around one feature, which is why they are easy to confuse. The difference is what the feature is and where the settlement sits relative to it: in a radial pattern the settlement occupies and surrounds the centre, while in a circular pattern the centre is water, which the settlement cannot occupy and must ring instead.

| Point of difference | Nucleated settlement | Dispersed settlement |
|---|---|---|
| Also called | Compact or clustered settlement | Scattered settlement |
| Spacing between houses | Houses are built close together | Houses are spread far apart |
| Form | The settlement forms a single closely built group | The settlement has no single built-up core |
| Reason the chapter gives | Security concerns favoured the evolution of nucleated settlements, in the past when areas were conquered or attacked frequently by outsiders | Arises where the physical setting or the pattern of landholding spreads people out |

Both are types of settlement, classified by the spacing between the houses, along with semi-clustered or fragmented settlement and isolated settlement.

[Note: the chapter gives the reason for nucleated settlements explicitly but does not state a corresponding cause for dispersed settlements, so that cell follows the physical and social factors it sets out earlier rather than a statement about dispersal.]

Draw a road, a railway line, a canal or a river running across the sheet, and place the houses in a single line along one or both sides of it, following its shape wherever it bends.

Label the line itself with what it is, for example 'Road' or 'River', label the houses, and title the diagram 'Linear settlement'.

The two features to get right are the ones the chapter names: the settlements occur along a road, railway, canal or river, and they lie in a straight line or take the shape of the road or the river. Keep the houses to the line and leave the ground away from it empty.

Draw a central object in the middle of the sheet, for example a temple, a market or a road junction, and label it 'central point'. Draw several routes leading outward from it in different directions, and place the houses along those routes so that the whole settlement spreads outward from the centre.

Title the diagram 'Radial settlement'.

The two features the chapter names are that the settlements grow around a central object or centre, and that this central point plays an important role in the development of the settlements around it, so the centre should be drawn first and everything else arranged with reference to it.

Draw a single closely built group of houses, with the houses touching or nearly touching and the lanes between them narrow, and leave the land all around the group empty, showing it as fields.

Label the built group 'compact settlement' and the surrounding land 'agricultural land', and title the diagram 'Compact settlement'.

The defining feature is the spacing: the chapter classifies settlements by the spacing between the houses, and a compact or clustered or nucleated settlement is the type in which they are closest together. It adds the reason such settlements arose, that security concerns favoured their evolution in the past when areas were frequently conquered or attacked, so a compact settlement is often drawn as one tight block.

Draw the houses singly or in twos and threes, spread widely apart across the whole sheet with fields or open ground between them, and with no single built-up core anywhere.

Label the individual houses and the land between them, and title the diagram 'Dispersed settlement'.

The contrast with the compact settlement is the point of the diagram: both are types classified by the spacing between the houses, and here the spacing is at its widest. Take care not to let any group of houses become a cluster, or the diagram becomes a semi-clustered or fragmented settlement instead.

Between 2005-06 and 2015-16 Lonar city grew outward, and the land it grew onto was wasteland-scrub rather than farmland.

On the earlier map the bright pink residential area is a single block north-east of Lonar Lake, with a fringe of salmon sparse-residential land around its southern edge and Lonai Village standing apart from it as a small dark red rural patch. The ground between and beyond them is light pink wasteland-scrub, with pale yellow agriculture further out. The lake itself sits inside a ring of olive-green forest.

On the later map that residential block is visibly larger, and a band of residential and sparse-residential land now runs south-east from it, past Lonai Village, to reach a new settlement named Krishna Nagar. Lonai Village, which stood on its own in 2005-06, has been absorbed into the edge of the built-up area.

The second change is in what the city contains. The 2005-06 map names almost nothing but the city, the lake, two villages and two temples. The 2015-16 map adds a Central Public School, a Civil & Criminal Court, a Tehsil Office, a Rural Hospital, a Gov. Hostel and a Gov. ITI, all of them purple public and semipublic land. So the city did not merely spread; it acquired administrative, educational, judicial and medical functions it did not have before.

What has not changed is the lake and its setting. Lonar Lake, the forest ring around it and Saraswati Village to the north-west look the same on both maps, and the built-up area has grown away from the lake rather than towards it.

This is the process the chapter describes twice over. Cities carry out more than one function as they grow, and one of these may be a major one; and the changes that come with growth show themselves as a change in land use and structure of the city.

The passage mentions hamlets, villages, small towns, large towns, isolated places, cities and conurbations. It also names the categories urban, suburban and rural, and gives a refugee camp as an example of a temporary settlement and a city as an example of a permanent one.

On the basis of precise definitions laid down by the authority doing the classifying. The passage gives the U.S. Census Bureau as its example, which divides settlements into urban or rural categories based on precise definitions.

The qualities those definitions rest on are given in the passage as population, density and access to services: small settlements such as hamlets and villages have low populations and restricted access to services, while larger types such as cities have higher populations, higher densities and greater access to services.

The passage says that types of rural settlements may be classified by function, and names farming, fishing and mining as the activities they may be close to.

It adds that a settlement which focuses on one economic activity is called a single functional settlement, which is the form many rural settlements take.

The difference is in the range of services a settlement offers, and it follows from its size.

A low-order service settlement is a small one, such as a hamlet or a village. It has a low population and restricted access to services, and the passage's example is a village with only one or two general stores.

A high-order service settlement is a large one, such as a city. It has a higher population, a higher density and greater access to services, and the passage's example is a large metropolis with many specialized stores and chain stores.

The practical consequence is dependence. The passage notes that larger settlements have a sphere of influence affecting surrounding settlements, so people in a low-order settlement travel to a high-order one for whatever their own does not provide.
